🌬️ Journey of One Breath — the map

  • Conducting portion: carries air to/from the gas-exchange sites. Nasal cavity → Nasopharynx → Larynx → Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Terminal bronchioles.
  • Respiratory portion: where gas exchange (O2 & CO2) actually happens. Respiratory bronchioles → Alveolar ducts → Alveolar sacs → Alveoli.
Vestibule = keratinized→non-keratinized stratified squamous. Respiratory area = pseudostratified ciliated columnar + goblet cells. Olfactory area = pseudostratified ciliated columnar, NO goblet cells (neuroepithelium).
Respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar + goblet cells).
3 epithelium types: respiratory; non-keratinized stratified squamous (vocal cords, epiglottis tip); neuroepithelium (taste buds, posterior epiglottis).
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar + goblet cells, on a thick distinct basement membrane.
Bronchi: same as trachea, decreasing in height/thickness. Bronchioles: epithelium simplifies step-by-step — pseudostratified → simple columnar → simple cuboidal (ciliated, then non-ciliated/Clara) as airways narrow, and goblet cells disappear.
Simple squamous (Type I) for gas exchange + cuboidal (Type II) for surfactant. No cilia, no goblet cells here — just thin membrane for diffusion.
👆 Tap any station to see how its epithelium changes along the way. Notice the trend: tall/complex → short/simple as airways get smaller.

👃 Station 1 · Nasal Cavity Histology

  • Wall, outside→in: Skin → Striated muscle → Cartilage → Bone → Mucous membrane (epithelium + corium)
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium → then transitions to non-keratinized. (Skin-like — this is the "doormat" that meets the outside world.)
Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells = classic "respiratory epithelium." Cilia + mucus = the conveyor-belt that sweeps trapped particles back out.
Pseudostratified columnar ciliated, no goblet cells, and no distinct basal lamina → it's actually neuroepithelium (smell-sensing nerve tissue, not just a lining).

🧠 Olfactory Epithelium — 4 cell types

🔧 Mechanism: smell signal pathway

Odor molecules → cilia of olfactory cells → signal travels down the olfactory nerve axon → through the cribriform plate → synapses in a glomerulus in the olfactory bulb → relayed by a mitral cell → olfactory tract → brain.

Fusiform bipolar neuron, perpendicular to the surface. Dendrite ends in a knob giving rise to olfactory cilia (the actual smell sensors). Nucleus in lower half. Function: senses odors.
Tall columnar, microvilli at the free surface, joined to olfactory cells by junctional complexes (except gap junctions). Rich in SER/Golgi/lysosomes/lipofuscin. Nucleus pale, upper half. Think: metabolic support cell.
Small, conical/round, sit on the basal lamina but don't reach the surface. Poorly-developed organoids, dark nuclei. Function: stem cells — divide & differentiate into supporting cells (this is how the lining regenerates).
Few in number, thick short apical microvilli. Probably carry ordinary (non-smell) sensation.

🔽 Station 2a · Nasopharynx Histology

  • Lined by respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar + goblet cells)
  • Corium: C.T. rich in elastic fibers, mucous glands, lymphatic tissue (pharyngeal tonsils); supported by bone + skeletal muscle

🎤 Station 2b · Larynx Histology

Mucosa — 3 epithelium types

🔧 Mechanism: epithelium matches local stress

Wherever two surfaces rub together during speech/swallowing (vocal cords, epiglottis tip), the lining switches to tough non-keratinized stratified squamous — just like it does at the esophagus. Everywhere else stays classic respiratory epithelium.

  • Respiratory epithelium — most of the larynx
  • Non-keratinized stratified squamous — anterior surface, epiglottis tips, vocal cords (friction zones)
  • Neuroepithelium — taste buds on the posterior epiglottis surface
  • Corium: loose C.T. rich in elastic fibers, lymph nodules & glands
  • Cartilages: Hyaline — thyroid, cricoid, arytenoid. Elastic — cuneiform, corniculate, epiglottic

🔧 Mechanism: why the epiglottis needs elastic cartilage

Elastic cartilage springs back to shape — perfect for a structure that has to bend down over the airway every single swallow and then pop right back up. Hyaline cartilage (thyroid/cricoid/arytenoid) instead gives rigid, stable support for the framework and the vocal ligament attachments.

  • Muscle: striated, extrinsic + intrinsic groups
  • Adventitia: loose C.T.

🎶 Vocal cords — false vs true

False cords (vestibular folds)True cords (vocal folds)
PositionUpper pairLower pair
EpitheliumRespiratory epitheliumStratified squamous
VascularityVascularAvascular
RoleNo vibrationVibrate to make sound

🔧 Mechanism

Being avascular keeps the true vocal cords pearly-white and lets them vibrate thousands of times per second without bleeding or swelling from friction.

🫧 Station 3 · Trachea Histology — 5 layers

1️⃣ Mucosa▾
Epithelium: pseudostratified ciliated columnar + goblet cells. Thick, distinctive basement membrane. Lamina propria: loose C.T. rich in lymphocytes, plasma cells, mast cells, eosinophils, fibroblasts, elastic fibers, vessels, lymphatics, seromucous glands.
2️⃣ Elastic membrane▾
Boundary between lamina propria & submucosa — not resolved by routine H&E stain.
3️⃣ Submucosa▾
C.T. with blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves, and mixed tubuloalveolar (seromucous) glands.
4️⃣ Cartilage & muscle▾
Hyaline cartilage as 16–20 C-shaped rings, open posteriorly. Fibroelastic fibers + smooth muscle (trachealis muscle) fill that posterior gap.

🔧 Why "C"-shaped, not a full ring?

The open back lets the adjacent esophagus bulge slightly forward as a food bolus passes — a full rigid ring would obstruct swallowing.

5️⃣ Adventitia▾
Thin connective-tissue outer layer.
👆 Tap each layer to expand it.

🌳 Station 4 · Bronchi

  • Trachea → 2 extrapulmonary (primary) bronchi → penetrate lung hilum → secondary (intrapulmonary) bronchi → continues branching, smaller & more numerous
  • Extrapulmonary bronchi wall ≈ same as trachea

Intrapulmonary (secondary) bronchi wall

  • Mucosa: as trachea, but epithelial height & lamina propria thickness decrease as bronchi get smaller
  • Muscularis mucosa (NEW layer appears here): continuous circular smooth muscle in larger bronchi, looser in smaller ones
  • Submucosa: loose C.T., glands present in larger bronchi
  • Cartilage: discontinuous plates (not full rings like trachea) — shrink as bronchial diameter decreases
  • Adventitia: moderately dense C.T.

🌿 Bronchioles

🔧 Mechanism: the airway "strips down" as it narrows

As airways branch and shrink, 3 things disappear in order: cartilage, then glands/goblet cells, then (eventually) cilia — while circular smooth muscle becomes proportionally more prominent. Less structural support is needed (smaller tube = inherently less likely to collapse), but more precise muscular control of diameter is gained.

  • Absent here: cartilage, goblet cells, glands, lymphatic nodules
  • Mucosa: starts pseudostratified columnar ciliated (no goblet cells) → gradually becomes simple columnar ciliated → simple cuboidal ciliated → simple cuboidal non-ciliated (Clara cells) in the smallest bronchioles
  • Muscle: circular smooth muscle, well developed
  • Adventitia: thin loose C.T.
FeatureBronchiBronchioles
EpitheliumCiliated + goblet cellsCiliated, no goblet cells
CartilagePresentAbsent
GlandsPresentAbsent
Smooth musclePresentProminent
LumenLarger, irregularSmaller, round

🔚 Terminal Bronchioles & Clara (Club) cells

  • Smallest/last part of the conducting portion
  • Lining: ciliated cuboidal cells, no goblet cells, but with Clara cells

🔧 Clara (Club) cell function

  • Non-ciliated, dome-shaped apical bulge (LM)
  • Protein-secreting ultrastructure: well-developed basal RER, supranuclear Golgi, apical SER, secretory granules
  • Secondary source of pulmonary surfactant
  • Secretes glycosaminoglycans that protect the bronchiolar lining

💨 Station 5 · Respiratory Bronchioles

  • Narrow diameter, lined by cuboidal epithelium
  • Initial segments: mix of ciliated cells + Clara cells; distally, Clara cells predominate
  • Scattered alveoli start budding directly off the walls here — this is the first true gas-exchange tissue encountered along the tube

🕳️ Alveolar Ducts & Sacs

  • Alveolar ducts: distal extension of respiratory bronchioles, lined by simple cuboidal non-ciliated epithelium; many alveoli open into them; the atrium = the duct's distal end, opening into alveolar ducts/alveoli/sacs
  • Alveolar sacs: clusters of alveoli opening into a shared space; typically at the end of a duct, but can occur anywhere along it

🫧 Station 6 · Alveoli & Interalveolar Septa

  • The structural + functional unit of respiratory tissue
  • Opens into an alveolar sac, duct, or respiratory bronchiole
  • Connected to neighbors by alveolar pores (pores of Kohn)
  • Separated by interalveolar septa; lined by Pneumocyte Type I + Type II

🔧 Mechanism: pores of Kohn

Tiny holes between adjacent alveoli that (1) equalize air pressure, (2) provide collateral ventilation if one alveolus's feeding bronchiole gets blocked, and (3) let alveolar macrophages migrate between alveoli.

🔧 Mechanism: interalveolar septum fibers

  • Elastic fibers → stretch on inspiration, then passively recoil on expiration (this passive recoil is a big part of how you breathe out at rest)
  • Reticular fibers → scaffolding that prevents over-distension / damage to the delicate capillaries
  • Fibroblasts ("septal cells") → make collagen III, elastin, proteoglycans of the septal matrix

Alveolar macrophages

  • Dust cells: phagocytose inhaled dust particles
  • Heart-failure cells: phagocytose red blood cells that have leaked in (seen in pulmonary congestion from heart failure)

🧱 Pneumocyte Type I

  • Very thin, flattened simple squamous cells — line most of the alveolar wall
  • Flat nucleus bulging into the lumen; sparse organelles (few mitochondria/ER) — it doesn't need to do much metabolically, just be thin
  • Tight junctions + desmosomes between neighbors → seals the barrier, prevents tissue fluid leaking into the alveolar air space
  • Basal lamina fuses with the capillary endothelium's basal lamina → shortest possible diffusion distance

🔧 Function

Pure structural gas-permeable surface — the "window glass" of the blood–air barrier. Thinness = fast diffusion.

🧫 Pneumocyte Type II & Surfactant

  • Cuboidal, central round nucleus; only ~3% of alveolar surface area (but outsized importance!)
  • Attached to Type I cells by tight junctions + desmosomes
  • Cytoplasm packed with lamellar bodies — large, electron-dense, multi-lamellar granules rich in phospholipid, glycosaminoglycans & protein
  • Well-developed Golgi, many mitochondria (lots of active synthesis happening)

🔧 Mechanism: 5 jobs of surfactant

  • Reduces surface tension → prevents alveolar collapse, especially at low lung volumes
  • Increases lung compliance → less effort, more air in per breath
  • Bactericidal effect → helps inhibit/kill certain bacteria
  • Maintains clearance → reduces protein/debris buildup
  • Stabilizes alveoli → keeps them open and evenly sized together
  • Also: Type II cells are the stem cell for both Type I and Type II pneumocytes — they repopulate the alveolar lining after injury

🧹 Alveolar Macrophages (recap)

  • Free cells within the alveolar space — not fixed to the wall
  • Dust cells (particles) vs heart-failure cells (erythrocytes, in heart failure/congestion)
  • Migrate between alveoli via the pores of Kohn

🚧 Blood–Air Barrier

  • The barrier gas must cross between alveolar air and capillary blood
  1. Film of pulmonary surfactant on the alveolar surface
  2. Cytoplasm of Type I pneumocyte
  3. Fused basal laminae of Type I cell + capillary endothelium
  4. Cytoplasm of capillary endothelium (non-fenestrated here)

Only ~4 layers, extremely thin → this is the side gas actually diffuses across.

On the opposite side of the capillary, the two basal laminae stay separate (not fused) and there's a true interstitial space in between — this "thick side" is where fluid/solute exchange happens, keeping the thin gas-exchange side dry and pristine.

🎯 Self-Test Quiz

From your lecture's own quiz — tap an answer to check yourself.

1. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the respiratory epithelium?
\n\n\n\n
💡 Respiratory epithelium = pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells — found from the nasal cavity down to the bronchi.
2. Which structure is present in the wall of a bronchus but absent in bronchioles?
\n\n\n\n
💡 Bronchioles lose cartilage entirely — that's their defining histological feature versus bronchi.
3. Which of the following is a characteristic feature of terminal bronchioles?
\n\n\n\n
💡 Terminal bronchioles are the last purely conducting segment — no cartilage, no glands, no alveoli yet.
4. Respiratory bronchioles can be distinguished from terminal bronchioles by the presence of:
\n\n\n\n
💡 Respiratory bronchioles are the first segment where scattered alveoli actually bud off the wall — true start of gas exchange.
5. Which alveolar cell type is mainly responsible for gas exchange?
\n\n\n\n
💡 Type I pneumocytes are thin and cover most of the alveolar surface — built purely for diffusion.
6. Lamellar bodies are characteristic of:
\n\n\n\n
💡 Lamellar bodies store surfactant components (phospholipid/GAG/protein) inside Type II pneumocytes.
7. Pulmonary surfactant is important because it:
\n\n\n\n
💡 Surfactant lowers surface tension, which is exactly what keeps small alveoli from collapsing (Laplace's law in action).
8. Which of the following cells may be found freely within the alveolar spaces?
\n\n\n\n
💡 Alveolar macrophages roam free in the air space itself — everything else listed is a fixed structural cell.
9. The pores of Kohn are important because they:
\n\n\n\n
💡 Pores of Kohn connect neighboring alveoli — pressure equalization, collateral ventilation, macrophage transit.
10. Which of the following is a component of the blood–air barrier?
\n\n\n\n
💡 The fused basal laminae of the Type I cell and the capillary endothelium are a key part of the thin gas-exchange barrier.
